title: Select, use and care for hand tools and basic equipment and infrastructure

lessons.title: Choosing the right tool for the job
lessons.html:
The right tool makes work easier and safer

On a farm you use many hand tools and simple equipment. Using the right tool saves time and stops injuries and broken tools.

JobTool or equipment
Digging holes and trenchesSpade, pick, crowbar, post-hole digger
WeedingHoe, garden fork
Levelling soilRake
Moving soil, manure or feedWheelbarrow, shovel, fork
Cutting branches and pruningSecateurs, pruning saw, loppers
Cutting grass and bushSlasher, sickle, panga, brush cutter (trained users)
FencingFencing pliers, wire strainer, hammer, droppers
WateringHose, watering can, knapsack for water
MeasuringMeasuring tape, line and pegs

Choosing well

  • Ask your supervisor what the job is and which tools to take.
  • Choose the right size: a short spade for small holes, a long one for deep digging.
  • Check the tool before use: handle not cracked or loose, blade sharp, no rust on moving parts.
  • Never use a tool for a job it was not made for. For example, do not use a spade as a lever to lift a rock; use a crowbar.
  • Take only the tools you need, and carry them safely.

Example

Your team must plant 50 fence droppers along a camp. You take a crowbar to break hard ground, a spade to clear the hole, a measuring tape and line to keep the spacing even, fencing pliers to tie the wire, and gloves for everyone. Taking the right tools means no trips back to the store.

Basic infrastructure you work with

Infrastructure means the fixed things on the farm: fences, gates, kraals, water troughs, pipes, sheds and tool stores. You use them every day. Close gates behind you, do not climb on fences, and report broken parts.

lessons.title: Using tools safely and solving problems
lessons.html:
Safety measures

  • Wear PPE: safety boots, gloves, hat; safety glasses when cutting, chopping or striking.
  • Keep a safe distance from other workers, at least the length of your tool swing, when using hoes, pangas or picks.
  • Carry sharp tools with the blade pointing down and away from your body. Never carry them on your shoulder in a group.
  • Cut away from your body.
  • Stand firmly with feet apart when digging or swinging.
  • Lift with bent knees and a straight back. Do not overload a wheelbarrow.
  • Never leave a rake or fork lying with the teeth up.
  • Do not use tools when you are very tired; take short rests and drink water.
  • Only trained workers use powered equipment such as brush cutters.

Recognising and acting on problems

ProblemAction
Loose spade or hoe headStop using it; tighten or report; a flying head can injure someone
Cracked or splintered handleStop; replace the handle
Blunt bladeSharpen it or ask for it to be sharpened
Flat wheelbarrow tyreReport and pump or repair
Rusty, stiff secateursClean and oil
Leaking hose or tapClose the tap and report
Broken gate or fenceReport so animals do not escape

Never try to repair something you were not trained to repair. When in doubt, take it out of use, put a sign on it, and tell your supervisor. A small problem fixed early saves a big problem later.

If someone is hurt

Stop work, call the first aider, and report the accident. Report near misses too.

lessons.title: Maintenance and safe storage
lessons.html:
Routine maintenance

Look after tools every day and they last for years.

  1. Clean: knock or scrape off soil and plant sap after work. Wash with water if needed.
  2. Dry: wipe tools dry so they do not rust.
  3. Oil: rub a little oil on metal parts and moving joints, like secateurs and pliers.
  4. Sharpen: keep hoes, spades, pangas and secateurs sharp with a file or sharpening stone, as you were shown. Wear gloves and push the file away from your body.
  5. Check handles: sand rough wooden handles smooth; rub them with linseed oil if your farm does this.
  6. Tighten: tighten nuts and screws.
  7. Wheelbarrows: check tyre pressure, grease the wheel, clean out the bin.
  8. Disinfect: clean pruning tools between plants or lands when there is disease, if instructed.

Storing equipment correctly

  • Return every tool to the store at the end of the day. Count them if the farm uses a tool list.
  • Hang long-handled tools on racks or hooks, blades up off the floor or covered, so nobody trips or gets cut.
  • Keep sharp tools in covers or in a rack where hands cannot touch the blades.
  • Store small tools in boxes or on shelves.
  • Keep the store dry and tidy, with walkways clear.
  • Keep chemicals and fuel in their own separate stores, not with hand tools.
  • Lock the store if the farm requires it.
  • Put broken tools aside with a label for repair.

Caring for infrastructure

  • Close gates and latch them.
  • Keep troughs clean and report leaks.
  • Do not lean heavy things on fences.
  • Keep sheds and kraals clean and report damage.

Key points

  • Choose the right tool and check it before use.
  • Carry sharp tools blade down and keep a safe distance from others.
  • Take broken tools out of use and report them.
  • Clean, dry, oil and sharpen tools after work.
  • Store tools safely on racks in a dry, tidy store.
